title: Kermer and colleagues · expected and actual emotions after a coin flip

blocks.text: **Kermer and colleagues (2006)** asked whether people can accurately predict how they will feel after a win or a loss. Participants first rated their baseline happiness and were given $5. They were then told that a coin flip would either win them another **$5** or lose them **$3**, and their predicted feelings before the flip were compared with their actual feelings afterward.

Beforehand, people expected losing $3 to drop their happiness by about **4 points** and winning $5 to raise it by about **2 points**. Afterward, the real drop from losing was only about **1 point**, and the real rise from winning was about **1.2 points**.
children: The expected loss was about twice the expected gain, even though the loss was the smaller amount of money.

blocks.text: People overestimated how bad a loss would feel because they ignore the **coping mechanisms** that get activated and soften it. These inaccurate **expected emotions** feed **risk aversion**.

title: Simonsohn · cloudy days, admissions, and enrollment

blocks.text: **Simonsohn** asked whether the weather, an **incidental** factor, carries over into important decisions. The manipulated factor was cloudy versus sunny days, either on the day of an admissions decision or on the day a student visited a campus.

**Simonsohn (2007)** analyzed university admissions decisions and found that applicants' academic attributes were weighted more heavily on **cloudy** days than on sunny days. **Simonsohn (2009)** looked at prospective students visiting a highly rated university and found that those who visited on a **cloudy** day were more likely to enroll.
children: 2007 is admissions decisions, and 2009 is enrollment by visitors.

blocks.text: The weather has nothing to do with the applicant or the school, yet it changed important decisions, which shows that incidental emotions can shape choices.

title: Lerner and colleagues · mood and highlighter prices

blocks.text: **Lerner and colleagues (2004)** asked whether a mood unrelated to a decision can change how much an object seems worth. Participants first watched a film clip that was **sad** (a person dying), **disgust** (a person using a dirty toilet), or **neutral** (fish at the Great Barrier Reef). They then set a selling price and a buying price for a set of highlighters.
For **selling**, neutral was about **$4.50**, disgust about **$2.70**, and sad about **$3.00**. For **buying**, neutral was about **$3.50**, disgust about **$3.00**, and sad about **$4.50**.
children: Disgust lowered both prices, while sadness lowered the selling price but raised the buying price.

blocks.text: The clips had nothing to do with the highlighters, so these were **incidental emotions**, and they still changed how much the same object seemed worth.

title: Physicians · earlier cases and cesarean recommendations

blocks.text: This study asked whether the **context** of earlier cases changes a decision about the very same case. Physicians judged one hypothetical cesarean test case in three contexts: alone first as the **control**, after four cases with **serious complications**, or after four **fairly routine** cases. The measure was whether they recommended a cesarean section for the test case.
**Significantly more doctors recommended a cesarean after reading the non-serious cases first.** The test case itself never changed, and only the cases that came before it did.
children: The cases just considered changed how the same patient was judged.

title: Organ donation · opt-in and opt-out consent

blocks.text: This comparison asked whether the way a choice is presented changes how many people become organ donors. In an **opt-in** procedure a person must take an active step to be a donor, while in an **opt-out** procedure a person is a donor unless they request otherwise. The measure was the consent rate in countries using each procedure.

Opt-in countries have consent rates **under 28 percent**, while opt-out countries have consent rates **over 99 percent**. Doing nothing makes a person a non-donor under opt-in but a donor under opt-out.
children: The default, not the people's wishes alone, decides the result.

blocks.text: This is the **status quo bias**, the tendency to do nothing when a decision is difficult.

title: Tversky and Kahneman · the disease problem in gain and loss frames

blocks.text: **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)** asked whether describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses changes risk-taking. A disease is expected to kill 600 people. In the **gain frame**, Program A saves 200 for certain, while Program B has a 1/3 chance that all 600 are saved and a 2/3 chance that none are saved. In the **loss frame**, Program C means 400 die for certain, while Program D has a 1/3 chance that no one dies and a 2/3 chance that all 600 die.

In the gain frame, **72 percent** chose A, the sure option, and 28 percent chose B. In the loss frame, **78 percent** chose D, the gamble, and 22 percent chose C. Yet **A and C are the same outcome**, since saving 200 of 600 means 400 die, and **B and D are the same gamble**.
children: Only the wording changed, and most people switched from the sure option to the gamble.

blocks.text: This is the **framing effect**: gains push people toward **risk aversion**, and losses push them toward **risk taking**.

title: Sanfey and colleagues · the ultimatum game and the anterior insula

blocks.text: **Sanfey and colleagues (2003)** asked whether emotion and brain activity explain why people reject unfair offers that cost them money. In the **ultimatum game**, a proposer splits money and the responder either accepts, so the money is divided as offered, or rejects, so neither player gets anything. Offers were $5/$5, $7/$3, $8/$2 or $9/$1, and each participant played 20 games, 10 with a human partner and 10 with a computer partner. The researchers recorded acceptance or rejection and activation of the **right anterior insula**.

$5/$5 and $7/$3 offers were accepted almost always. An $8/$2 offer was accepted about **53 percent** of the time from a human versus **85 percent** from a computer, and a $9/$1 offer about **37 percent** versus **68 percent**. More right anterior insula activation meant rejecting more offers.
children: Participants were angrier at an unfair human than at an unfair computer.

blocks.text: **Utility theory** says to accept any offer, because any money beats nothing, but people reject and give up money. Emotion, here anger at unfairness, is important in decision making.

title: Belief bias · judging invalid believable conclusions

blocks.text: This research asked whether a believable conclusion makes people accept a syllogism as valid. Participants judged **invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions**, and the measure was whether they called them valid.
**71 percent** judged these invalid syllogisms as valid. This is **belief bias**: people judge by whether the conclusion sounds true instead of whether it follows from the premises.
children: Sounding right is not the same as following.

blocks.text: Take *All of the students are tired; Some tired people are irritable; therefore Some of the students are irritable*. Every statement sounds fine, but the conclusion does not follow, so the syllogism is **not valid**.

title: Conditional syllogisms · four forms and accuracy

blocks.text: This research asked which kinds of if-then syllogisms people judge correctly. All four forms start with **If p, then q**, and they differ in the second premise: **p** (modus ponens), **not q** (modus tollens), **q**, and **not p**. Participants judged each form as valid or invalid.

**Modus ponens** was judged correctly **97 percent** of the time, **modus tollens** 60 percent, and each of the two invalid forms, **syllogisms 3 and 4**, only **40 percent**. Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid ones.
children: Modus tollens is just as valid as modus ponens, yet much harder.

blocks.text: Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid, and syllogisms 3 and 4 are not.

title: Wason four-card problem · abstract and concrete versions

blocks.text: This research asked whether using real-world items makes conditional reasoning easier. In the **abstract version**, the cards read E, K, 4 and 7, and the rule was that a vowel on one side means an even number on the other. In the **concrete version**, the cards read Beer, Soda, 16 years old and 21 years old, and the rule was that drinking beer means being 21 years old. Participants chose which cards to turn over.
In the abstract version, **46 percent** chose the 4, which is an error, and only **7 percent** chose the correct 7. In the concrete version, **73 percent** answered correctly.
children: The correct cards are E and 7 in the abstract version, and beer and 16 years old in the concrete version.

blocks.text: Following the **falsification principle**, you look for cases that could break the rule, so the 4 and the 21 cannot help. **Permission schemas** in familiar rules make this easier.
